X. ELECTION/APPOINTMENT OF CITY OFFICIALS None. XI. REPORT OF CITY OFFICERS None. XII. EXECUTIVE COMMUNICATIONS Legal Expense Analysis Report for the period July 1, 2026 through September 15, 2026. Assistant Solicitor Verdecchia was present to answer questions. There were no questions. No action needed. XIII. COUNCIL PRESIDENT COMMUNICATIONS None. XIV. COUNCIL MEMBER COMMUNICATIONS Councilman Ritz • Update from the Administration regarding the Oaklawn Ave. flooding. Councilman Ritz asked whether the meeting between RIDOT and the Mayor had taken place and whether a temporary warning solution was available. Director Moretti stated that the flooding is a joint City-State problem, as most of the water entering Wilbur Avenue comes from Oaklawn Avenue, a State road; that the Mayor had requested a meeting with the Acting RIDOT Director the following day; that a permanent fix would be a multi-million-dollar project; and that he would look into why the flashing warning lights did not activate and into additional safety measures. Councilwoman Graziano recommended applying for an EPA Section 319 nonpoint source grant and other stormwater grants, cautioned against raising the road, and suggested underground storage and subsurface infiltration. Director Moretti noted the Council has a grant writer available to it. Councilman Traficante asked that the entire length of Oaklawn Avenue be reviewed. Council President Wall stated the item will remain on the October agenda for an update. • Update from the Administration regarding their meeting with Waste Management. Director Moretti stated that the local Waste Management staff are responsive but residents must reach a national call center, where bin and lid replacement requests are handled under the “billing” prompt; that the City is in year one of a five-year contract; that the bins have a ten-year life and are fourteen years old; that a citywide replacement would cost roughly $2 million; and that just under 1,000 blue and gray bins are on order for the second or third week of October. Councilman Ritz asked for a smaller follow-up meeting with Waste Management. Council Vice-President Haroian cited stolen and lidless bins, rodent problems and approximately $663,000 in costs from rejected recycling loads, and recommended restoring the recycling education position in the next budget. Councilman Buonanno urged that the City be proactive and hold Waste Management accountable. Councilwoman Vaziri asked about bin barcodes. Councilwoman Graziano asked about the bin budget. Council President Wall noted, on advice of counsel, that discussion should remain within the agenda item. No action was taken. XV. COUNCIL BUSINESS MATTERS CARRIED OVER None. XVI. title: 05-26-01 Ordinance in amendment of Title 8, Chapter 08, Section 200, of the City of Cranston Code of Ordinances, 2005, Entitled “Outdoor Fires (Cooking Fires of Any Kind).” Sponsored by Council Vice-President Haroian
action: On motion duly made by Councilman Buonanno and seconded by Councilwoman Vaziri, it was voted to adopt the above Ordinance.
source_excerpt: On motion duly made by Councilman Buonanno and seconded by Councilwoman Vaziri, it was voted to adopt the above Ordinance. The following being recorded as voting “aye”: Councilwoman Graziano, Councilmen Andujar, Ritz, Traficante, Councilwoman Vaziri, Councilmen Campopiano, Buonanno, Council Vice-President Haroian and Council President Wall -9. Under Discussion: Council Vice-President Haroian stated outdoor heaters and fire pits were brought forward by the Fire Marshal so the Fire Department would know where open gas is in use at restaurants and could have some form of inspection. She stated the Fire Department asked that items be inspected, that they not simply be purchased without a nationally recognized testing laboratory listing, and that the ordinance would mimic the State Fire Marshal’s requirements. Solicitor Millea stated Section C.1 refers to a nationally recognized testing laboratory and does not itself say anyone will go out and inspect. Discussion followed that subsection C.1 had been amended after the hearing with the Fire Department. Solicitor Millea stated subsection C.3 reads as if equipment is being installed by the Fire Marshal and should read that it shall be inspected by the Fire Marshal once installed; he described the change as not substantive. In response to whether the ordinance could be passed as is and later changed, he indicated it could be passed and he would recommend the clarifying change. Councilwoman Graziano stated she was furious that comments were arriving as the Council was about to pass an ordinance that had already been through the process more than once, and that she needs comments well ahead of time from the Solicitor. Councilman Buonanno stated Attorney Marcello’s advice to get the law on the books was prudent, that even a comma would send it back to committee, that the matter had already been sent back once, and that he would vote it as presented and edit later rather than continue to punt it for grammar. Council President Wall concurred, stating the Fire Department wanted it in place and outdoor cooking fires would not be as pertinent a safety matter if delayed until December. Roll call was taken on motion to adopt the above Ordinance and motion passed on a vote of 9-0. The following being recorded as voting “aye”: Councilwoman Graziano, Councilmen Andujar, Ritz, Traficante, Councilwoman Vaziri, Councilmen Campopiano, Buonanno, Council Vice-President Haroian and Council President Wall -9. 6-15-01 Ordinance in Amendment of Title 10, Chapter 12, Section 130 of the City of Cranston Code of Ordinances, 2005, Entitled “Right Turns at Certain Red Lights.” Sponsored by Councilman Buonanno. title: 1. Resolution Authorizing the Placement of Ballot Questions to be Presented to the Voters at the General Election to be held on November 3, 2026
action: On motion duly made by Councilwoman Haroian and seconded by Councilman Andujar, discussion opened.
source_excerpt: On motion duly made by Councilwoman Haroian and seconded by Councilman Andujar, discussion opened. Under Discussion: Councilman Buonanno agreed the items are needs rather than “nice to haves.” He stated placing the questions on the ballot is one of several steps before money is borrowed or spent, that voter approval in November would still leave further Council and Administration action, and that he would not be on the Council at that later stage. He asked the public not to treat this evening’s vote as a vote to borrow. Councilman Traficante stated that in each category there is still bond authority left from previous bonding and that remaining prior authority should be expended first. Council Vice-President Haroian echoed the Council President, citing school boilers, roofs draining into classrooms, and the need for funds in an emergency. She stated the Council learned during the year about grant spending and a fountain project that lacked oversight, that she has spoken with the Council President about closer oversight, and that the bonds are for necessities. She noted she is a taxpayer. Councilwoman Graziano echoed her colleagues, stating flooding, roadways, schools and safety services are serious, that checks and balances were part of the capital-budget vote requiring the Council to revisit bonding and seek financial information before spending, and that she supports oversight of project management and RFPs. Councilman Ritz supported his colleagues and stated a large share is for schools, which he said keep and grow the City’s tax base, citing roofs and boilers discussed in a recent presentation. Councilman Campopiano stated he went back and forth on adding debt, that it is for the voters to decide, and asked the Finance Director what the tax impact would be if the full amount were used. Finance Director Robert Strom stated a million dollars at 4% on a 25-year bond would cost the City roughly $65,000 annually in principal and interest; $51 million if totally used would cost roughly $3.2 million per year; some bonds could be interest-only in the first year. Councilman Campopiano asked about using the sewer fund for storm drains if language were changed. Attorney Marcello stated that when the capital budget was passed the Council made clear that any and all projects would have to come back before the Council for approval before money is borrowed, and that voter approval authorizes up to the stated amount but does not require spending that amount. Using parks as an example, he said a $4 million parks authorization could be used later for a $500,000 project if so authorized. Councilman Campopiano asked how much project-level discretion the Council would have, citing a school magnet-board purchase. Council President Wall stated the fountain situation showed the Council would want specifics and would not give carte blanche. Councilman Traficante asked whether the sewer fund remains an enterprise fund and whether the City can take from it. Director Strom stated the City can borrow from the fund but it must be repaid, not taken permanently. Councilman Campopiano clarified he meant crossover between sewer and drainage. Director Renzulli stated that before former Solicitor Chris Rawson passed away he drafted an ordinance that would make some stormwater work from the sewer enterprise fund legally possible; that ordinance has not been presented because it needs further work with the current Solicitor; until such an ordinance is passed she does not believe the Administration intends to use the sewer fund other than as it is used now. Director Moretti stated such an ordinance may have been drafted but has not been discussed with the Mayor, would require vetting, and that money assessed for sewer cannot presently fund drainage; interest income from the sewer fund, not principal, was determined during budget season to be usable for operating purposes and need not be paid back into the fund. Councilman Buonanno stated the sewer discussion was a rabbit hole unrelated to placing bond questions on the ballot. Council Vice-President Haroian stated for the record that she found it interesting Councilman Campopiano knew about a sewer-fund ordinance that others on the Council, including the Council President and Finance Chair, did not. Council President Wall stated the sewer fund is not on the agenda and returned the body to the bond questions. The questions discussed, totaling approximately $51 million as stated by the Finance Director, correspond to the General Assembly enabling acts previously supported by the Council: storm drains and drainage ($4,000,000); playgrounds, athletic fields and related equipment ($4,000,000); public buildings ($2,000,000); streets, sidewalks and bridges ($8,000,000); fire and public-safety equipment ($8,000,000); and schools and school facilities ($25,000,000). Roll call was taken on motion to adopt the above Resolution and motion passed on a vote of 9-0. The following being recorded as voting “aye”: Councilwoman Graziano, Councilmen Andujar, Ritz, Traficante, Councilwoman Vaziri, Councilmen Campopiano, Buonanno, Council Vice-President Haroian and Council President Wall -9.

If he’s not mistaken, and he wants to be sure, it’s always protocol, before you release any bonded money, that it be brought before the Council for their consideration. In these times especially, before increasing the debt service, Council wants to make sure, even though we have the ability, that it’s absolutely necessary. This Council may not deem everything in that capital budget as necessary at this time. That will be the protocol going forward. We can still go out to bond for the money, but the money is not spent until it is approved by Council. Council President Wall asked Director Strom to provide clarification for the record. Just because you have the ability does not mean you necessarily have to release it. This Council may not deem everything in that capital budget as necessary at this time. That will be the protocol going forward. Councilman Campopiano stated Council has heard many people in the gallery talk about a moratorium on capital expenses. Just to clarify, we do not need a moratorium. We have a system of checks and balances where Council will approve anything going forward as far as capital projects. We can still go out to bond for the money, but the money is not spent until it is approved by Council. Council President Wall asked Director Strom to provide clarification for the record. Director Strom had this discussion today with Councilwoman Graziano. When the city goes out to bond, there’s a list of the items we want to bond for. That’s when they come before Council; to get approval for the particular items we are going to bond for in particular projects. We also go out for just authority. When we do that, it does not mean we have to go to bond. We could hold off for two to three years. It’s not because you get the authority that you have to bond for that amount. The other thing, as far as debt service, when we got out and do an actual bond, we try and incorporate it so that it does not affect our debt service and it’s over maybe a two-year period and the first year may be just interest only. It may not be principal and interest. We try to schedule it so it’s advantageous to the city from a financial standpoint. Council President Wall thanked Director Strom. He liked the simple answer that Council is the checks and balances. Councilman Buonanno stated there is a lot of confusion by the public that reducing some of the items in the capital budget will decrease the tax levy. He knows that’s not the case. He asked Director Strom to explain it. Director Strom stated one is capital and one is the operating budget. It’s two different things. The only thing that affects the operating is debt service and we control that debt service as much as we can because we don’t bond for everything that’s been approved in the capital budget. Some of that gets deferred to next year or even the year after depending on the urgency and need for the capital item. Councilman Buonanno gave the example of the track. Removing $2 million from the capital budget and making it zero does not give the city an extra $2 million in the operating budget. That’s a very important point for the public to understand. When we eventually pass the capital budget of almost $22 million, that’s not coming out of the tax bills. It’s not something we can take and give to the senior center and the schools and CCAP. He would like Director Strom to explain why it doesn’t work that way. Director Strom reiterated because one’s not related to the other. One’s capital and one’s operating. The only thing that affects the operating is debt service and debt service is based on what’s already been bonded and what we’ve received in proceeds to do certain projects. He does not know where those numbers came from, but what was expended is what was required to be paid for our debt service and that was over budget by a considerable amount of money. That’s based on the schedule of our debt service, both principal and interest and it also shows on the sewer principal and interest as well, but the main thing in the operating budget is the principal and interest. Discussion: Councilman Buonanno noted the increase will not necessarily be 4.99%. That is the backstop. Everything is still on the table. Councilman Ritz had a hard time passing 4.99%. It is a last resort to fix the problem. For weeks he has listened to residents and reviewed the impact of cuts. He hoped to receive a budget with a 5% reduction in operating expenses. He would be more comfortable with a 4% max increase. Even 4.5% provides key services while still respecting the taxpayers. He believes money can be found to restore the Senior Center and provide additional support to the schools. Realistically, the Senior Center may need to operate leaner. The schools will still be doing more with less. He would like a breakdown from the Senior Center of what a 10% reduction in operations would look like, while preserving core functions. During the tour he would like to meet with each division to understand their functions, and what services are truly essential. His MBA is in lean operations. He manages budgets and operational efficiencies daily in his professional life. He offered to collaborate with any department. He thinks it would help the body if the school administration provided a tiered scenario of what an additional $1 million, $1.5 million, or $2 million would look like. He understands there is already a plan in place for level funding. He would like a barebones breakdown from the CCAP Administration of how funds are used and the direct impact on residents. He would like to meet with their administration. We now have additional time with the delay to June 1. That time should be used productively. He and his colleagues will continue to identify efficiencies and cuts to balance the budget while restoring items without putting it on the backs of the taxpayers. To recap, he is more comfortable with a 4-4.5% increase or less; he wants to restore the Senior Center, but likely in a leaner form; he would like to provide additional funding to the schools, but with a clear breakdown of where that money will be used; he wants transparency around CCAP funding and impact; and he wants direct meetings and tours to better understand operational realties before making final decisions. Every department needs to have the mindset that they need to contribute something as Council works toward a balanced and responsible budget. He suggested the Administration operate on a “cash diet”. Councilman Traficante agrees with Council President Wall and Councilman Andujar on the limitation. It would be unfair to allow this budget to be balanced on the backs of school children and seniors. Every department has a responsibility to the citizens of Cranston to participate and assist. Council President Wall stated Council cannot go beyond a 4.65% tax increase tonight. If Council passes the resolution and the General Assembly approves, when we come back on June 1, we could go up to 4.99%, if we need additional appropriations. He called for a vote. action: On motion by Councilman Buonanno, seconded by Council Vice-President Haroian, it was voted to adopt the above Ordinance.
source_excerpt: On motion by Councilman Buonanno, seconded by Council Vice-President Haroian, it was voted to adopt the above Ordinance. Under Discussion: 2026-03-16/Rosalba/CouncilMinutes/2026/2026_04_20 Councilman Campopiano stated that he does not know if it is possible to delay this or tap the brakes, but there is a lot of uncertainty in the City right now and he does not know if he can support this without knowing what is going forward. They do a wonderful job and it is nothing against them, but he does not know where we stand. He is asking if it is possible to put this off, if not, he is not going to be able to support it. Councilman Campopiano motioned to table this Ordinance. No one seconded the motion. Councilman Traficante stated that he will recuse from voting on this because he is a member of the New England Laborers Union and was also a former member of Local 1322. Council President Wall stated that when this came before Committee, he did mention when this came up that although they are small raises within this collective bargaining unit, ultimately, these are mechanics and tradespeople who save the School Department money. He was in favor of it. Usually, he is against any increases at this point just because in this expenditure, we actually save because if we had to go out in the open market for the skill set of the members of this collective bargaining unit possess, it would cost us exponentially more. This is why he will support it this evening. He sees Mr. Crudele in the audience and asked if he had any information he would like to share with the Council. Michael Crudele, Chief Human Resources Officer for the Public Schools, appeared to speak and echoed what Council President Wall stated. The amount that is in the fiscal impact included in the Council’s packet does not even come close to what it would cost if we had to contract this work out. They have 23 buildings, 3 plumbers, 2 electricians, 2 carpenters and 2 HVAC people that handle all 23 buildings. It is a huge task and they do it flawlessly on numerous occasions. They have also been asked by the City to work with Parks and Recreation. They have put up safety lighting at a few of the facilities. They also have four mechanics in this group, who are working constantly on our fleet of buses, which is approximately 85 buses handled by four mechanics. If they were to go out and contract this work it would not even come close to what you see in the fiscal impact. Councilman Campopiano stated that he is not faulting them, he is not saying they do not do a good job, they do a wonderful job, but at this present time, he would just feel more comfortable if it was just delayed. We have to face our constituents, it would just be easier to defend if it was just after we knew what was going on and everything was settled and revisited and he is sure it would be no problem whatsoever. Mr. Crudele stated that he is a taxpayer himself and totally understands, but he just fears that the deficit we are looking at would be that much greater if they contracted outside and they lost these men. Councilman Ritz stated that he agrees that the timing on this is tough, but having been a former School Committee Member, he knows this is a small group and a skilled group so to lose them without this small increase, he thinks is a tougher loss to the City. He agrees that it saves us more money than having to not only send this work out but then retrain people into this, is the balance here. Mr. Crudele stated that there are thirteen members in this unit and financial impact for 2026-2027 was $112,863. Council Vice-President Haroian stated that she thinks we are all a little uneasy with this like Councilman Campopiano said, but having been on the School Committee, realizing that this is thirteen people, these men are specially trained and we are dealing with School buses. We are in financial trouble is an understatement, but she will be supporting this this evening. Councilman Campopiano stated that he is not saying no, he is just saying table to next meeting. Roll call was taken on motion to adopt the above Ordinance and motion passed on a vote of 6-1. The following being recorded as voting “aye”: Councilwoman Graziano, Councilman Ritz, Councilwoman Vaziri, Councilman Buonanno, Council Vice-President 2026-03-16/Rosalba/CouncilMinutes/2026/2026_04_20 Haroian and Council President Wall -6.
